text: 8:05. Intern Lisa is waiting outside your office with a notebook: "Can I just watch how you work?" Today you mostly planned to work on a crossword.
left: Let her watch, we'll solve it together

text: Your mentee Danya sends a nine-minute voice note at 7:40: "So, quick question." You're still in pajamas. Listen now?
Sonya asks for advice: a rival firm is offering her double the salary. Your company values her a lot. What's your honest advice?
A junior analyst shows you a dashboard with 47 charts: "It's all about sales." You understand exactly one, and it's about the weather. How do you react?
left: Ask to keep just three charts

text: In the evening Danya texts: "Today I told my boss 'no,' like you taught me. I think I'm getting fired now." That's not quite what you taught. Reply?
right: "Sleep on it, we'll fix it tomorrow"

text: The HR director wants to launch a mentoring program named after you. You'd personally coach 12 young employees. Wednesdays. For a year.
Intern Misha asks: "Is it true you started out fixing the printer?" The truth is you broke it back then. Tell the story?
left: Tell it exactly as it happened

text: A young manager asks for a call at 9 p.m.: "Five minutes, just about my career." In your experience, "just about my career" lasts ninety minutes. Agree?
Sonya sends her résumé for a review. Under "Hobbies" it says: "Being inspired by you." Flattering, but employers might be puzzled. What do you say?
The training team recorded your masterclass, but your sandwich keeps getting into the shot. The editor asks: cut it or keep it "for authenticity"?
Evening. You catch yourself saying "Back in my day…" to young staff for the third time today. Maybe time for a new catchphrase?
left: Start a fine jar for every "back in my day"

text: A junior designer wants feedback on their portfolio by 10: the interview is at 11. It's 80 slides and it's 8:30. What now?
left: Skim it and give three tips
right: Drop everything for a full review

text: Danya asks how you learned to speak without notes. Honest answer: you used notes for twenty years, you just wrote very small. Admit it?
left: Confess and show the cheat sheet

text: Sonya from marketing sends you a meme about yourself: "Is it OK if this becomes a sticker in the company chat?" It's you yawning in a meeting.
At 9:00 thirty graduates of the internship program are waiting in a meeting room. Each wants a selfie and "one question." The board meets in 40 minutes.
A junior lawyer brings a contract and whispers: "I found a senior partner's mistake but I'm scared to say." It's a serious one. How do you help?
left: Coach him to say it himself

text: The mentors' chat is debating whether you can text mentees after 8 p.m. You just sent three messages at 10:15. Your vote?
In the elevator Sonya asks: "How did you know when it was time to go home?" Honestly, you can't remember a single such day before last year. Answer?
Intern Misha writes down your every word. You said "I should get lunch" and he underlined it twice. It's a bit awkward. What do you do?
right: Ask him not to note everything

text: You realize you teach young people about balance while answering emails at 11 p.m. Your conscience stares back from the laptop screen. Close it?
HR asks you to personally give the office tour to newcomers. They expect a legend, and this morning you couldn't find your other sock. Go?
A young product manager offers to "level up your productivity" with an app that sends 14 notifications a day. Try it?
Danya invited you to his first talk at an internal meetup. Same time as a family evening you promised a month ago. Where to?
left: Talk, and bring the family a pie

text: Lisa asks you for a recommendation letter for her master's. She's been interning for three weeks; you mostly remember her notebook.
left: Write it after a proper chat

text: A junior developer argues with you in a stand-up and turns out to be right. Everyone freezes: nobody has publicly corrected the legend before. Reaction?
Sonya asks you to record a short evening video for her grandma: "She believes in you more than in me." You're tired and dinner's not made. Record it?
Sonya shows up with a spreadsheet titled "My 47 goals for the quarter." You remember making those at her age and burning out by March.
right: Let her learn on her own

text: The intern program lead complains: after your lecture three interns demand "the right to a quiet hour." The board isn't thrilled. Defend it?
Danya asks how you survived your first failure. You recall Project Phoenix, which burned down twice. Share the details?
The training team wants to turn your advice into an online course with quizzes. Question one: "What does the legend drink in the morning?" That's a bit scary.
A junior analyst is burning out, working late "to be like you." That's exactly how you once burned out. What do you do?
In the evening Misha sends "a list of questions for the legend tomorrow." There are 58, and the last one is: "Are you happy?" Start from the end?
Sonya asks you to attend her first board presentation "just to sit in the corner for support." The board will think you're pushing her. Go?
The corporate academy wants to name you "Honorary Mentor" and give you a gown. It's blue, with a tassel. Pose in it?
A young manager writes: "I want to leave for creative work, but I'm afraid to let you down." He's the best in his department. Reply?
Lisa brings you coffee "just the way you like it." You like tea, but everyone already says the legend drinks coffee. Come clean?
A junior developer asks whether to learn a fifth programming language or get some sleep. He asks at 3 p.m. with red eyes. Advice?
Someone posted an old photo from your first office party in the mentors' chat. You're dancing with a ficus. The youngsters demand details.
Danya asks if he can have your old chair: "A legend sat on it." The chair creaks and wobbles. Give it to him?
A department head complains your mentees are too bold: "They argue with me using your quotes." You feel proud and guilty at the same time.
Lisa sent an essay: "What I learned from the legend in a month." Point one: "You can leave at 6 p.m. and not die of shame." Share it in the newsletter?
A colleague who just became a mentor asks for your "template." You don't have one, you have a napkin with three points. Share it?
right: Sit down and write a manual

text: A young product manager wants you to be the "living brand" of his in-house startup: one photo with the product per week. Payment in cookies.
Sonya got promoted and thanks you on social media in three paragraphs. The chairman writes: "And what about us?" What do you do?
Misha came in at 6:50 to "work like you." Security calls: an intern is sitting in the dark in the lobby. What do you tell him?
right: Let him get used to it

text: A junior analyst brings an idea you tried 15 years ago, and it flopped. But times have changed. Reply?
left: "Try it, but keep this in mind"

text: It hits you that your mentees know more about your life than your relatives. Call your sister right now?
The CFO wants to halve the mentoring budget: "The youngsters adore you for free anyway." Push back?
right: Cut it, but keep the lunches

text: Your assistant Platon reports: today you have nine back-to-back 20-minute mentee meetings, no breaks. He "optimized." Redo it?
In an evening memo the board asks you to "spend less time on the youngsters and more on strategy." Your mentees read it before you did.
right: Invite the board to meet the youngsters

text: A publisher wants you to write a book about your career. Modest advance, six-month deadline, working title "Surviving Till Friday: A Memoir." Sign?
left: Sign, but with your own title
right: Take a year to think about it

text: Your editor Vera read chapter one: "Very honest. Too honest. Here you call the board 'a slide appreciation society.'" Remove it?
11:40 p.m. You've been writing the book for three hours and produced one sentence: "It all started with the water cooler." Keep going or sleep?
Your literary agent suggests a chapter called "My Morning Rituals." Your morning ritual is looking for your keys. Write it?
Accounting heard about the book and wants a chapter about them, on one condition: "Only about how we saved you during reporting season." Agree?
Your daughter reads the draft: "Two hundred pages about work and a footnote about us." The footnote really is tiny. What now?
Vera wants the chapter by Monday, but you promised the grandkids a fishing trip this weekend. You could write in the boat, but the fish won't approve.
The proofreader found 312 misplaced commas and one story she says "couldn't have happened." It's true. Prove it?
You're offered a co-writer to "retell your life vividly." His vivid language added a skydive that never happened.
right: Keep him, but check every page

text: The designer sent a cover: you, full-length, against a rising sun, holding a sword for some reason. You laugh; the publisher loves it.
The company lawyer flagged 40 places in red as "possible claims." Mostly they're just former colleagues' names.
You reread the chapter about your first year and realize you were very happy then, despite earning peanuts. Awkward for a book about career growth.
The publisher calls: "We need more drama. Did you have an enemy?" No enemies, just a printer that hated you. Will that do?
Fyodor found out he's in the book and asks to be "taller, with a mustache." He's never had a mustache. Give in?
Your son suggests you dictate the book and he'll transcribe it. In return he wants to be first in the acknowledgments.
Vera suggests titling the chapter on your biggest flop "The Lesson." You wanted "Oh Well." Who wins?
The publisher's marketer wants book merch: a mug saying "Friday is a state of mind." Not your quote, but it sounds like you.
right: Offer a real quote of yours

text: Your granddaughter wants her drawing in the book: you and the cat at work. The publisher is against pictures.
right: Hang it in your office instead

text: Your very first boss heard about the book and calls at 8 a.m.: "I hope I'm a good guy in it?" Actually, he's more of a comic relief.
right: Promise to send him a copy

text: The press office wants to approve the book "to avoid risks." In their version every project succeeded and you were never late once.
Vera sent 112 comments in the evening. The last one says: "All great, get some rest." You're not sure the first 111 agree.
Platon suggests blocking two hours every morning "for the book." But that's when you usually call partners. Block them?
Zinaida from accounting, who was there when you started, sent a photo of your very first payroll slip. Book material?
right: Keep it in the family album

text: A book blogger asks for an advance manuscript "for an honest review." He's famous for honestly trashing everything. Risk it?
The publisher wants "Bestseller" on the cover before it's even out. "Everyone does it." You feel a little ashamed.
Sales bought 2,000 copies of your book "as client gifts." Half of the clients have already gotten it twice.
Final chapter. You need to sum up what your career taught you in one sentence. So far: "Eat on time." Is that the wisdom?
Vera wants the book cut by a third. On the chopping block: the chapter about your cactus that survived three reorganizations. Cut it?
Timur, once your intern, now a director, sent a chapter "as I remember it." In his version you're strict but fair. Include it?
The family stages a read-aloud of your book in the kitchen. Everyone voices a character. The cat plays your first boss.
The printers say your cover photo came out green. Print run: 5,000. Reprint, or "it's kind of trendy"?
Vera suggests adding "tips for each day of the week." For Friday you have one tip: "Leave early." Enough?
You remember a time 20 years ago when you wronged a colleague. It's in the draft. You could leave it out and just call him instead.
Your agent proposes an audiobook narrated by you: 14 hours in a studio. By hour five your voice turns into a whisper.
Misha asks to borrow the manuscript "just to read at lunch." An hour later the general chat is quoting it, including the board chapter.
Your first reader writes: "Your book helped me quit a job I hated." You're glad, but not sure your HR director will be.
The publisher wants a book launch at 8 a.m. in a bookstore: "Perfect for business people." You've been a night owl for decades.
A translator asks how to render "survive till Friday" in other languages. He suggests "make it to the weekend." Something's lost.
The book is almost done, and you feel sad, as if your career itself is ending. Maybe it's not sadness but fatigue?
Vera suggests a foreword from a famous person. You want it written by Galya the cleaner, who's known you for 25 years.
The board asks you to "gently revise" the restructuring chapter. It describes you arguing until you were hoarse.
Your daughter wants to run a "My parent is writing a book" account with daily stories. You want quiet; she's beaming.
A bookstore invites you to a signing on Saturday at 10. Saturday at 10 is your swim, which you've skipped five times already.
HR wants to give your book to every new hire. It has a chapter on nearly quitting in your first month. Bad for onboarding?
A local book club picked your book and invites you to the discussion. They warn: "It can get rough." Go?
Sales are good and the publisher wants book two in six months: "On leadership, you know the drill." You know you want six months of quiet.
Vera admits she cried over the chapter on your first office party. You wrote it as comedy. Something went wrong, or right?
At night you think of a better title than the current one. But the cover's already at the printer. Call the publisher right now?
The cover photographer wants "a thoughtful gaze into the distance." In the distance: a parking lot and a man failing to park for ten minutes.
right: Do a hundred takes in the studio

text: A courier delivers the first copy of your book at 7:15. You're in the hallway in one slipper, crying. He waits for a signature, also a bit moved.
A major forum wants you as keynote speaker. Irony: 25 years ago you handed out badges at this very forum. Mention it on stage?
The panel moderator has talked for 18 of 20 minutes, all about himself. You have two minutes left. Interrupt?
right: Wait and use your two minutes

text: After the conference you're at the hotel, and you're invited to a "casual speakers' dinner" till midnight. The room, silence and slippers call louder.
The slide clicker is dead and the tech went for coffee. The hall's full, you're on stage. Say "next slide" out loud the whole time?
During Q&A a schoolgirl stands up: "Weren't you bored going to work for forty years?" The hall holds its breath.
After your third conference this week you forget which city you're in. The hotel doesn't say, and asking is embarrassing.
right: Look out the window and guess

text: A festival organizer wants you to walk on to your "signature music." You don't have any. They suggest a march.
The teleprompter suddenly switches to someone else's talk on pork logistics. You're six minutes into your speech.
Platon proposes accepting 14 conference invites in 9 cities this month. "It's fame!" The spreadsheet alone makes you dizzy.
The event stylist wants you in sneakers and a hoodie: "That's how leaders speak now." Your sneakers were last seen in eighth grade.
Your badge has a typo: you're now "Honorary Speeker." Half the hall has already photographed it. Fix it?
After the talk a man comes up: "Your lecture ten years ago made me become a baker." He's brought a baguette. Your car's waiting.
At 7:00 the organizers send a new format: instead of a talk, "40 minutes of interaction with the audience." You prepped the talk for three weeks.
The simultaneous interpreter asks you not to joke: "I can't keep up, the foreigners laugh a minute later." Your talk has 11 jokes.
right: Joke and pause for the echo

text: You're back from a conference Friday night, and the family has gone to the country house without you: "You're tired anyway." Catch up?
A student council asks you to speak for free to freshmen at 8:30 a.m. on a Saturday. Audience: 400 sleepy people.
A conference proposes you appear as a hologram instead of traveling. The hologram is half a meter shorter and slightly green.
At the speakers' party they ask you to dance "like in your legendary ficus story." The ficus story has reached another city.
The organizer asks you to cut your talk from 40 to 7 minutes: "Guests are tired." You flew 2,000 km.
Your lapel mic is caught on a button and the whole hall hears your stomach rumble. You skipped lunch for three back-to-back interviews.
The emcee introduces you as "the person who invented Friday." The hall laughs. Correct him?
Platon booked a 5:40 a.m. flight "so you can make the opening." You'd rather skip the opening and sleep.
Sonya is speaking at the same conference, next hall, same time as you. Her room is half empty. Send people her way?
left: Plug her talk from the stage

text: Someone posted a clip where you say "we should work less." Commenters argue whether you're a guru or a slacker.
A conference in the mountains: your talk is at 9, but sunrise and a trail start at 6. You can make the summit if you rush and skip breakfast.
A sponsor asks you to mention their product in your talk "naturally, in passing." It's a smart mop.
At a conference you bump into an old colleague from your very first department. He wants to "hang out like old times." Back then you stayed up till dawn.
The organizers give speakers a spa voucher, valid today 9 to 11, exactly during your talk.
You're speaking at a kids' career day, right after an astronaut and a vet. The kids are already yawning. How to save it?
right: Hand out candy and take questions

text: You notice you've told the same water-cooler story on stage for three years. The crowd always laughs. But you're bored of it.
The video engineer says your glasses glare on the big screen and suggests taking them off. Or is the glare rather symbolic?
A young attendee asks you to watch his pitch right in the hallway. Six more people start lining up behind him.
Platon texts at night: "Tomorrow you're expected at a conference you forgot you agreed to." He shows you your "yes" typed in an elevator.
The organizer wants you to open the forum by striking a giant gong. Last time the gong fell on a minister's foot.
The event's tech lead wants you to present with a robot assistant. The robot can only say "Please repeat that."
Your daughter watched your talk online: "You're funny on stage but not at home. Why?" Good question.
Another famous speaker asks to swap slots: 9 a.m. is inconvenient for him. For you too, but you're already up.
While you're at a conference, the office calls: "We decided to change the logo while you're away." You opposed it, and you're 3,000 km away.
The cabbie recognizes you: "You're the one who said work less? I don't work Fridays anymore." Is he in trouble now?
An online conference at 7 a.m. your time because it suits another time zone. The camera will show your kitchen and the cat on the table.
right: Get up earlier and tidy up

text: The forum photographer caught you mid-sneeze. The photo landed on the homepage. Ask for a replacement?
The organizer offers a fee or a lifetime free pass to the forum. You're not sure you want to attend even once.
right: Take the pass for your mentees

text: Platon prepared you an "all-purpose speech": openings, closings, anniversaries and funerals for ideas. Read it before you go on?
The moderator asks: "What advice would you give your 20-year-old self?" You want to say, "Buy a decent chair." Is that OK?
Three times this week you preached rest from the stage and didn't rest once. Cancel tomorrow's trip?
Your flight is delayed six hours and you speak tonight. In the lounge people recognize you and ask for a "mini-lecture."
The organizer pairs you on stage with an old rival who once stole your best client. The crowd wants sparks.
After the talk a woman says quietly: "I disagree with every word you said, but thank you." You'd love to talk, but the taxi's waiting.
The organizer asks you to sign 300 forum programs "for VIP guests" during a 15-minute break. Your hand already hurts.
The hotel mixed up bookings and your room went to a young first-time speaker. You're offered a room by the elevator.
A director wants to make a documentary about you, opening with you waking up. The crew can be at your home at 6 a.m.
The documentary's camera operator asks you to walk the hallway "once more, but pensively." It's take twelve and staff are applauding.
A popular podcaster invites you for a three-hour recording, "no edits, raw and honest." Honestly, you can't talk for three hours straight.
A business reporter asks: "Your main secret to success?" You suspect it was switching departments right when that one manager arrived.
Before going on air, the makeup artist draws your eyebrows "a bit more confident." A surprised stranger looks back from the mirror. Wipe it off?
The director wants to shoot "an evening at the legend's home": you reading by the fireplace. You have a space heater and a couch with a cat.
A morning TV show wants you in the studio at 6:30 to tell your career story in 3 minutes, between the weather and a pancake recipe.
A reporter asks: "Who would you fire if you could go back in time?" Your press secretary next to you turns pale.
Fyodor heard about the documentary and sent a 40-minute video memory. Half of it is about his vegetable garden.
A live radio host asks for your favorite song. You name the one from your car. Turns out it's a shampoo jingle.
Your press secretary brought 200 "possible questions" with prepared answers. The interview is in two hours, and lunch hasn't begun.
Platon asks if the film crew can come to Sunday family dinner. The family watches you from the kitchen very meaningfully.
A journalist wants the interview on a treadmill: "It's our 'run with a leader' format." You run once a year, and this year's run is done.
The director wants to restage your first job interview. The actor playing you is a head taller and way more confident.
Watching your own interview, you count 46 "actually"s. Actually, that's a lot. Keep watching?
right: Finish it and work on it

text: The documentary team wants to film accounting as "the place where the legend began." Accounting is mid-year-end close and not happy about guests.
right: Ask them to bear it for an hour

text: A TV channel pitches a reality show, "A Week with the Legend": cameras in the office for five days. The board is already rubbing its hands.
After the recording the podcaster asks for "five more minutes on your personal life." It's about your divorce twenty years ago.
A trainee reporter is doing the first interview of his life and shaking. His recorder hasn't been on for ten minutes.
right: Say nothing, send a text later

text: The camera operator asks to switch off the AC because "it's noisy." It's 31°C in the room and the interview has 90 minutes left.
Your daughter watched the trailer: "Why is there dramatic music for the work part and a sad little piano for us?"
At 7:20 a reporter calls: "Is it true you're retiring?" You haven't told anyone, not even yourself.
The press office prepared "three key messages." The reporter asks about your favorite food. Squeeze in a key message?
The director sends a rough cut: four hours long, forty minutes of which are you looking out a window. It's "a metaphor." Ask for cuts?
A student newspaper asks for an interview and warns they can only pay in cafeteria pies. The pies are said to be legendary.
A magazine photographer wants you on the office roof "with wind in your hair." There's a storm warning on the roof.
Mom saw your interview and calls: "You said you dreamed of being an accountant as a kid. What about space?"
right: Explain it had to be that way

text: A blogger with a million followers wants a "Day in the life of a legend in 60 seconds" clip. He wants you to drink coffee on a roof.
A correspondent asks about a former colleague you once clashed with. He's famous now. Talk about it?
Three interviews today, and in each you said family matters most. You haven't been home since morning. Call?
The director wants to film your commute by public transit, "like in your youth." You've driven for 15 years. Ride the subway?
A reporter asks about your salary. Your press secretary kicks you under the table. You did promise transparency.
A late-night host asks you to tell an office joke. You know one, but it's about your own board.
A journalist wants to interview you at your first office, which is now a café. The barista sells a "Legend Latte" at triple price.
The film needs a "conflict scene." The director suggests staging an argument with a subordinate. He's already practicing his angry face.
The podcaster sends a headline for approval: "The Legend Confesses: I Hate Mondays." You never said that.
A TV channel wants a live broadcast from your office at 8 a.m. Your desk has last night's pizza box and three mugs.
The film editor wants you to record voice-over. It's written in your voice but grandiose: "I am the office. The office is me." Read it?
right: Read it with a straight face

text: Your son says you've become a meme and shows it at dinner. It's funny, but you're "the boss capybara." Like it?
A correspondent wants to film "the legend's morning workout." Your workout is stretching in bed.
A reporter asks about your worst project. The press office said to discuss only achievements. Project Phoenix burned down twice.
After two months of filming the crew leaves. The house is suddenly quiet, and you almost miss the camera. Call them?
The interviewer opens with a lightning round: coffee or tea, office or remote, Friday or Saturday. You freeze on the third one.
The sound engineer asks you to repeat "The team is everything." You recall that "everything" used to mean deadlines. Say that?
The documentary premiere is set on your wedding anniversary. The director says without you "the hall will be empty."
A podcaster wants to record at 7 a.m. "while your voice is fresh." At 7 your voice usually sounds like a creaky door.
Asked about regrets, you said "skipped lunches." It became the headline, and now people send you sandwiches.
You told a reporter your first-day story for the fifth time. Each time it gets more heroic. The legend seems to be growing by itself.
A magazine fact-checker calls: "Is it true you once held a meeting in a stuck elevator?" True, and it was the best meeting ever.
A magazine put you on its "50 Most Influential" list and wants a superhero-costume photo for the cover. The cape arrived by courier.
Next week's calendar: 31 invitations, four of them at the same time on Wednesday. Your assistant asks where you'd like to "split in two."
right: Pick two and run between them

text: Platon wrote a polite decline template. It's so warm that two recipients think you're coming. Rewrite it?
Your country-house neighbor found out you're "that legend" and asks you to speak to the garden cooperative about "efficiency."
You're invited to cut the ribbon at a new business center at 8 a.m. The scissors are promised to be golden. The morning will be lovely without them.
The chairman asks you to be the face of a charity marathon. You don't have to run, just stand at the finish for six hours.
For the first time in your life you said "no" to an important invitation, and now you've stared at the ceiling for half an hour. Freedom or anxiety?
right: Write back that you changed your mind

text: Your old school invites you to host the first-day-of-school ceremony. The principal is your former classmate who copied your homework.
A restaurateur wants to name a dish after you and asks you to the opening. The dish is a three-cabbage salad.
A childhood friend writes: "You're a star now, probably too busy?" You really are busy, but it stings to read.
Platon says you've been invited to judge six competitions at once. One is a contest for best office pie.
A colleague from a regional office asks you to come "just to support the team." It's nine hours by train, and your granddaughter's art show is this weekend.
At 10:30 p.m. an unknown number calls. It's an organizer who "just wants to hear your voice and invite you to their company's anniversary."
A former colleague is getting married and wants you as guest of honor and toastmaster: "There'd be no wedding without you, we met at the water cooler."
A university wants a 25-minute commencement speech, "no shorter." The graduates want photos, not speeches.
The family proposes a new rule: after 7 p.m. your phone goes in the bread box. The bread box is small but strict. Sign up?
A gym offers a free membership if you let them hang your photo: "The legend trains here." You've never been there.
Marketing planned your quarter: 12 webinars, 4 podcasts and one bowling night with clients. Bowling is the only part you like.
You can't remember the last time you took a walk without a phone call. How about right now?
The chairman asks a "small favor": chair the corporate culture committee. Two hours a week, "three tops." You know what that really means.
A neighbor asks you to speak at her son's parent meeting on "how to succeed." He's six.
Platon asks if he can answer invites with "The legend is on vacation." You're not, but you'd love to be.
Your university's alumni club wants you as honorary president. Duties: "show up sometimes, pay sometimes."
A major partner invites you golfing "to discuss the deal." You can't play golf and are sure the deal needs fifteen minutes.
Your granddaughter asks why Saturday in your calendar just says "NOTHING" in capitals. You explain it's your most important meeting.
You're invited to a gala for the "Year of Efficiency." Evening dress, six hours, speech required.
Your very first boss invites you over "to talk about life." He warns there'll be slides about his seedlings.
Sixty-four "Got a minute?" messages came in tonight. You've learned not to answer after 8 p.m. Almost. One is from your mentee.
Platon asks how to answer invitations for three years from now. You don't know what you'll be doing then, but you hope it's fishing.
The company's anniversary party wants you on stage at 11 p.m. "for the finale." You've gone to bed at 10:30 for two years and loved it.
You count your declines for the month: 23 "no"s. No world ended. Keep going?
A local football club asks you to take the ceremonial first kick. The last time you kicked a ball was in school, and it went through a window.
Platon asks if he can tell organizers you have "a packed schedule" when you've actually scheduled a nap.
Your college friends are meeting on Saturday, the same day you're invited to open a tech park. You haven't seen them in ten years.
You're invited to "Name That Tune: Executive Edition." You can only identify shampoo jingles.
Accounting invites you to a small party for Zinaida's retirement. It clashes with an important investor meeting.
Your partner gently says: "We agreed you'd say no, yet Saturday has three yeses." Shows you the calendar.
Platon suggests delegating some invitations to your mentees: "Let them grow." They're scared but thrilled.
The city wants to name a bench by the office after you. You ate lunch there for twenty years. There's a plaque unveiling.
You skipped dinner with important people for a TV series with your cat. And you're not ashamed at all. Is that OK?
Marketing wants short greetings for 40 different events, each naming the city and the organizer.
The chairman asks you to host foreign guests for "just three days." The program: ballet, a factory, and a fish market at 5 a.m.
Your son texts: "Coming to my birthday or is it 'a conference' again?" You check the calendar: a conference again.
right: Come for the end of the party

text: An organizer writes: "Your name is already on the poster, too late to back out." You never agreed to anything.
right: Go, but this is the last time

text: A colleague your age confesses: "I said yes my whole life and don't remember my forties." He asks you to teach him to say no.
Platon's year-end report: you declined 300 times and took two vacations for the first time. The company didn't collapse. Frame it?
A 7 a.m. breakfast with "young leaders," titled "Early Birds." You're an owl.
Platon asks if he can book over your "lunch with myself" slot. It's the head of a huge foreign delegation.
A school textbook wants your portrait in a "Careers of the Future" section. There's a photo shoot and a quote for kids.
An invite to an "exclusive dinner of business legends." The other legends are people you've argued with in meetings for twenty years.
The alarm rings at 6 a.m. though everything today is cancelled. You forgot to turn it off: you haven't had an empty day in years.
Your grandson Lyova jumps on the bed at 7 a.m.: "You promised we'd build a rocket today!" You did, and there's also a board call at 9:30.
The family chat is voting on summer plans: sea, mountains, or "wherever Grandpa/Grandma gets no signal." Option three is winning.
Your partner proposes an evening with no work talk. In the first ten minutes you've started "By the way, at the board…" three times.
Your daughter asks you to drop her kid at daycare because she has an important meeting. The irony: she's adopting your lifestyle.
Mom calls mid-meeting for the third time. Usually it means "buy bread," but once it meant "it's my birthday."
Your cat Ponchik lay on the keyboard and emailed the board "aaaaaaaaaa." The board replied: "We support this." Explain?
Your granddaughter Masha asks at breakfast: "What do you do at work?" You try to explain and she dozes off into her porridge.
left: Tell it as an office fairy tale

text: Your son wants to start a business and asks not for money, "just advice." That'll take three hours, and you have a 4 p.m. call.
Anniversary. Your partner gifted you a "phone-free weekend" voucher, effective today at 6 p.m.
Your sister calls at 7:30: "You know I learned about your book from the paper?" You meant to tell her. For six months.
left: Apologize and give her a copy
right: "It was meant to be a surprise"

text: Lyova came for "bring your grandkid to work day" and already ran a meeting with sales. Sales are delighted.
The family suggests a monthly board-game night. The very first time you start optimizing the property-trading game rules. Everyone objects.
Your partner suggests an alarm-free morning. Your body wakes at 6 by itself and reaches for email. Resist?
Mom saw you on TV and is hurt: "Why no hello to your mother in the interview?" It's not done in the news, but…
left: Say hi in the next one

text: Your daughter is job hunting and asks to list you as a reference. She's brilliant, but the shared surname makes it awkward.
Masha drew you a "weekend pass" with a potato stamp. It says: "Today: home." Today is Tuesday.
A photo in the family chat: your grandson took apart your old laptop "to see where reports live." It held a 15-year archive.
Your partner admits: "I'm proud of you, but I miss who you were before the board." You want to answer honestly.
Your son sends a video of his first work presentation. It got a "good." You see yourself in him, mistakes included.
Your dog Tuchka learned to open the office door during video calls. Today she joined the investor call carrying a sock.
Lyova's homework is "My family's jobs." He writes: "Grandma/Grandpa works as a legend." The teacher wants specifics.
Mom asks you to drive her to the market Saturday at 7 a.m., "like before." Before was 30 years ago, when you never slept.
Your daughter complains about her boss. You recognize yourself from twenty years ago. Tell her?
Dinner. Everyone stares because you're on time for the first time in a month. Someone suggests a commemorative photo.
Your partner signed you up for a pottery class on Saturday. Without asking. You'd planned to "do a bit of work."
Masha calls from school: she's been elected class monitor and wants to "consult the top boss." You're in negotiations.
The neighbor complains your late-night typing is so loud he can't sleep. Your laptop is typing a book.
Your son offers a smartwatch to remind you to "stand up and walk." You suspect it'll also remind you of meetings.
The family assigns holiday duties. Yours: "Don't organize anything, just show up." Do you feel useless, or free?
Your partner puts on your favorite film from your youth. At minute twenty you check email. Your partner hits pause and stares.
Lyova asks if he can take your "Legend of the Year" award to show-and-tell. It's heavy and made of glass.
Your sister asks you to get her son into your company, "even as an intern." He's a good kid, but you're against favoritism.
Your daughter asks how to leave work on time when her boss texts at 9 p.m. You're texting your deputy at 9:03.
left: Delete the text to your deputy

text: Mom mailed a newspaper clipping about you, circled everything and wrote: "Eat your soup." Best thing in the morning mail.
Your partner suggests moving to the countryside once you step back. You love the city, but you love quiet too. Decide now?
Masha wants a bedtime story. You read her the sales report because the book's in the car. She falls asleep instantly.
right: The report is a fairy tale too

text: The family asks who's making weekend breakfast. The last time you cooked breakfast was in the fax era.
Your son asks you, for the first time, not to come to his work event: "Everyone will just stare at you." It stings but makes sense.
Lyova watched the documentary about you: "Why are you so serious in the movie?" You don't know either.
Tuchka's been waiting for a walk since 6:30 and has brought the leash, your shoe and your tie. You need the tie for the 9 a.m. board meeting.
Your partner texts: "Remember we have our routine checkup together today?" You vaguely do. There's a press conference at that time.
Your grandson started a "Legend Quote of the Day" thread. Today's: "Where are my glasses?" Forty reactions.
Your partner's weekend plan: no laptop, the woods, pie. Friday night the board writes: "Got a minute this weekend?"
right: Give them an hour on Saturday

text: Your daughter became a manager and asks if the boss must always leave last. You did it for 30 years.
Mom calls: "You work so much. Come for pies." The pies are 300 km away. Tomorrow's a day off.
Masha asks if she can become "a legend like you." You want her happy, not legendary. What do you say?
Lyova is selling lemonade at the school fair and wants advice on his "growth strategy." His competitor is the pie stand opposite.
Your partner found a box of your old ID badges from every job. There are 34. Toss them or have a memory night?
Your sister proposes a three-day trip together to your hometown, like when you were kids. Those three days are quarterly reporting.
For a week Ponchik the cat has been sleeping in your work briefcase. You need it for a big meeting; the cat clearly considers it his office.
You joined an amateur choir. Rehearsal is Saturday at 10, and the board just set an "informal breakfast" for the same time. Where do you sing?
Your art teacher says your still life with apples "looks a lot like an org chart." Is that a compliment?
Evening fishing, silence, a bite. Your phone buzzes: your deputy can't find the budget file. It's in your email, on your phone.
You've decided to bike to work. It's 14 km, the office has no shower, and you meet investors at 9:30.
Your mug from pottery class came out lopsided. The teacher says, "It's wabi-sabi." You want to give it to the chairman.
At the chess club you lose three games in a row to a nine-year-old. He offers a rematch and "a little coaching."
The zucchini at the dacha ripened. Forty of them. You brought some to the office and accounting already begs "no more." How to give away the rest?
Your Italian class asks you to describe your job. You only know "pasta," "opera" and "Friday."
You dug out a guitar you haven't played in 30 years. Your fingers remember three chords, your neighbors remember silence. Play?
You got up at 5 to shoot the sunrise over the river. The birds are gorgeous, but your phone shows 14 unread from the office.
A beekeeper friend offers you a hive "to try out." The board heard and asks whether it's a conflict of interest with the cafeteria honey.
You decided to master cooking and made dinner from a video recipe. It's twice the amount and three times saltier. The family bravely eats.
You signed up for a 5 km run. Colleagues found out and placed bets. The bets are on you walking it.
Platon asks if your watercolor lessons should go in the shared calendar. Then everyone will see you "paint clouds" on Wednesdays.
In the workshop you built a stool. It's sturdy but looks a bit like an elephant. Friends suggest an exhibition; a neighbor wants to buy it.
You signed up for tango. Your dance partner is a former subordinate. He leads confidently and won't let you take charge.
You spot a rare bird from the meeting-room window mid-presentation. Your binoculars are in your bag.
You're invited to a retirees' mystery book club. You're not retired, but you love mysteries more than business books.
Your yoga teacher asks you to "let go of your thoughts." You let go of all but one: "Did we send the report?"
You've been building a model sailing ship. In a meeting people notice glue on your fingers and thread in your hair. Explain?
A group of retirees invited you to Nordic walking at 7 p.m. You're the youngest and the slowest.
For the first time in 20 years you wake without a work thought. Your first thought is what color the new flower bed will be. Change is afoot?
At a bread-baking workshop you argue with the chef about "fermentation strategy." Other students just want bread.
You paint in the evenings, and one watercolor ends up online. A gallery offers an exhibition. The board worries about your image.
The dacha tomatoes need watering every morning. At 7 you have a call with a branch. Hose or laptop?
left: Take the call in the garden

text: You're learning a tune on the piano in an empty auditorium at lunch. The entire sales team walks in for a training.
You finally watch the show everyone recommended seven years ago. In episode three the hero has the same boss you once had.
At your first lesson the swim coach asks how far you can swim. You honestly say: "To the edge."
The chairman learns you collect stamps and offers a swap. His stamp is clearly worth more, and the trade is clearly diplomatic.
You're doing a 3,000-piece puzzle. One piece is missing and you suspect the cat. The cat looks innocent. Search the flat?
Your first time at a climbing gym, and the instructor is your intern Misha. He yells: "Reach for it like a strategic goal!"
A branch wants a video meeting. You're at a ceramics workshop, clay up to your elbows.
You bought a telescope. The sky only clears at 2 a.m. The board meets at 9.
right: Set an alarm for tomorrow night

text: Your language-exchange partner is a student who has no idea who you are. It's the most relaxed conversation you've had all year.
Platon found "Knitting, 2 hours" in your calendar and asks if it's a typo. It's not; it's a scarf for your granddaughter.
Your dacha neighbor learns you managed thousands and asks you to help "organize" her husband to dig potatoes.
You notice you have five hobbies and a KPI plan for each. Maybe hobbies should just be for joy?
Your dahlias took third place at the garden show. The ceremony is at 3 p.m.; so is a board session.
right: Ask a neighbor to pick it up

text: You bought an online course called "How to Learn to Do Nothing." It has 12 modules and homework. The irony is palpable.
The choir director offers you a solo at the concert. It's Friday night, and the whole office already bought tickets.
The workshop says restoring your grandmother's dresser will take three months of Saturdays. For once you want a long project with no deadline.
Weekend fishing: in the next boat is a former rival who also left "for the quiet." He suggests teaming up on a business.
Colleagues propose a company bike ride with you leading. Your bike remembers three rides; the route is 50 km.
An amateur theater invites you to play a strict director. The director says you "won't even need to act." Offended?
You do cross-stitch and accidentally stitched the company logo on a pillow. Your hand did it by itself. Unpick it?
left: Unpick it and stitch a cat
right: Gift the pillow to the office

text: The chairman heard about your choir and wants it to perform at the annual shareholders' meeting. The choir mostly sings about birch trees.
The CFO notices you leave at 4 p.m. on Thursdays for ceramics and asks to move the budget committee to… Thursday at 4.
Your tennis coach suggests an amateur tournament. Your first-round opponent is a board member. Play to win?
The board proposes a corporate trip "into nature with the legend." You'd dreamed of nature without the board.
You wake to find moles dug up the lawn overnight. Tomorrow the lawn hosts your own brainchild: a "garden meeting" with investors.
right: Get up at 5 and level the lawn

text: The chairman says it's time to pick a successor by year's end. The shortlist: deputy Oleg, product director Anna, and your mentee Sonya.
left: Start a shadow week with each

text: During shadow week Oleg notes everything, including where you hide cookies. He's clearly prepping for more than strategy.
right: Ask him to focus on business

text: Anna sends a 30-page "First 100 Days" plan in the evening. You haven't left, and she's already planned your office.
Sonya finds out she's on the successor shortlist and panics: "I'm not ready, but I don't want to let you down."
The HR director proposes an assessment center: two days of tests, cases and role-play. Candidates are already terrified.
You realize you don't want to pick a successor, because then you'd have to admit you're leaving. Delay another month?
Oleg shows up at 7:30 with coffee and suggests "discussing the handover before everyone gets in." It's coffee you don't like.
Anna asks for access to your correspondence with key clients "for a smooth transition." No decision's been made yet.
Your partner has listened to your successor agonizing for an hour: "Flip a coin and notice what you hope for while it's in the air."
A headhunter pitches an outside candidate: "A star, 38, three successful companies." Your three internal candidates heard before you did.
The board wants a successor "like you, but younger and cheaper." You look in the mirror, unsure if that's a compliment.
Sonya sends an idea in the evening that solves a problem you've fought for three years. She writes: "Probably silly."
The receptionist whispers that the candidates are already splitting up your people. Oleg took legal to lunch; Anna took sales.
right: Let them show what they've got

text: Oleg asks if you'll leave him your office with the park view. The view is your favorite part of the job.
You've made a candidate comparison table. Under "Will they be happy in this job?" everyone has a question mark. Is that column important?
Anna proposes a test: give her full authority for a week. That week is annual reporting.
The CFO whispers: "Oleg's reliable but dull; Anna's a genius but will fire everyone; Sonya's lovely but young." Thanks, very helpful.
Oleg invites you fishing, "no work talk." Two minutes in he asks where the safe password is kept.
Staff ran an unofficial poll, "Who'll be the new boss?" They didn't ask you, but sent you the results first thing.
In a meeting Anna sharply scolded an intern. An hour later she comes to you: "I overdid it. How do I fix it?"
Lyova heard you're picking "the new boss" and offers himself. His pitch: "I can build rockets." The most honest candidate yet.
right: Offer him the job in 20 years

text: Sonya asks: "If it isn't me, tell me first. I don't want to find out from a memo." Fair.
The lawyer reminds you the successor must be approved at a meeting and suggests drafting three orders "just in case."
At night you realize none of the candidates will be "like you." And maybe that's a good thing.
Oleg's plan: keep everything as it was under you, "break nothing." The board wants change; the staff want stability.
The receptionist asks whether to replace your door sign "in advance, to save time." It's ordered, but without a name.
Anna confides she's afraid of becoming "a legend": too much responsibility. You understand better than she thinks.
The chairman pushes: "Decision by Friday." It's Monday and you haven't talked to the candidates one-on-one.
left: Talk to all of them today

text: Sonya comes with an idea: "What if Anna and I worked together? She's strategy, I'm people." The board never considered that.
left: Pitch the tandem to the board
right: Say it doesn't work that way

text: Your partner says: "You're choosing a successor like you're picking someone to adopt your child." Surprisingly accurate.
Oleg was late to the last shadow-week meeting because he drove his daughter to school. He apologizes for the third time.
HR brings psychometric results: Oleg "stability," Anna "ambition," Sonya "empathy." Under your name it says "departing."
Timur, now a director himself, calls: "Want succession advice from someone you once picked?" Turns out you picked him 15 years ago.
The board wants to announce the successor at your farewell party, "two events in one." You suspect the evening won't be about you anymore.
Oleg asks for a reference "in case it's not me." He's already eyeing jobs elsewhere.
You've chosen. Now you have to call the two who weren't picked. Harder than any deal in 30 years. Call tonight?
Learning it's not her, Anna holds up well but asks for a project "where nobody will teach me."
News of the successor leaked before the announcement. Staff whisper, the board's annoyed, and the successor is hiding in a meeting room.
Your new successor calls at 10 p.m.: "Can I call you every evening for another year?" You've dreamed of call-free evenings.
Your successor runs the stand-up for the first time while you sit to the side. He makes a mistake you know by heart. Step in?
Your successor asks for a "survival guide." You sit down and realize it all fits on one page.
Sonya, not chosen, writes: "Thank you for not picking me. I think I can breathe again." Be glad?
Oleg, staying on as deputy, offers the new boss your old desk "out of respect for tradition." It wobbles.
The board offers you an "honorary advisor" role after you leave: two days a month, a badge, an office. Tempting and dangerous.
In six months your phone will go quiet. That's scary and wonderful at once. Which is stronger?
Your successor asks to replace your beloved "Friday pie" ritual with "Friday smoothies." Staff are in turmoil.
Your successor made his first decision you disagree with. Not a disaster, just not yours. Speak up?
For the first time you don't know what's happening in the board meeting. You want to call "just to check." Call?
Your successor asks for all system passwords. They're in a paper notebook with kittens on it, and half no longer work.
right: Sit down and reset them all

text: Platon asks if he gets "inherited" by the successor. He'd rather stay with you and help with the book.
You visit your first office for the film. The same water cooler still stands in the corner, gurgling as ever. A sign: "Here began the legend."
left: Pour a cup and stand quietly
right: Ask them to remove the sign

text: At the office reunion Zinaida from accounting pulls out a folder: "Your 2004 business trip expense report. The receipt was never submitted."
right: Admit the debt and hug her

text: At the reunion your first boss toasts: "I always knew this one would go far." You remember him saying the opposite.
Fyodor showed up an hour early and has told everyone he "taught the legend to use a stapler." Almost true.
Vika, once an intern, now has her own company and wants you as a consultant. You're proud, but you wanted to rest.
They found the old coffee machine you broke in your first week and gave it to you as a keepsake. It still doesn't work.
right: Give it to the office museum

text: The security guard at your first office recognizes you and asks for a pass. "Rules are rules, even for legends." You haven't had one here in 20 years.
The old sysadmin who once saved your report at 3 a.m. sits in a corner at the reunion. Nobody notices him.
Galya, who cleaned your first office, brought a photo: you asleep on the meeting-room couch in 2006. It's passed around.
Someone revived your first department's chat. Messages from 2008; the last one is yours: "Who took my mug?" Still no answer.
Timur confesses at the reunion that he took the mug. "I still have it. I drank from it at every big meeting for luck."
Your first boss pulls you aside: "I was too strict back then. Sorry." You've waited 25 years for this and don't know what to say.
In the old office storeroom they found the very printer you feuded with. Organizers suggest "a symbolic victory": print one page.
Your first company's accounting asks you to sign a 2003 payroll sheet missing your signature. Without it "the archive can't close."
Fyodor invites everyone "like old times" to the canteen across the street. It's now a trendy restaurant with old-time prices plus a zero.
Vika recalls you once told her, "Don't be afraid to make mistakes." She did: a million-sized one, and she grew. You don't remember saying it.
The HR person who hired you shows your old application. Under "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?" you wrote: "On vacation."
right: Ask them not to show it

text: That evening, after everyone's gone, you linger by the cooler. It gurgles as if trying to say something. Probably "finally, get some rest."
right: Call your deputy on the way home

text: Your first boss asks you to help his grandson with a résumé. It opens: "My grandfather was the legend's boss."
Zinaida retired and now keeps the books for three neighbors' cats. "They pay on time, unlike you back then."
right: Give her a box of chocolates

text: After the reunion you realize your best memories aren't deals but lunches by the cooler. Bring the lunches back?
left: Start them at the new office

text: Fyodor calls in the morning: "Let's meet monthly, or we'll die without finishing our conversation." Dramatic, but true.
Timur wants you to speak at his company. His staff already know the mug story and await the living legend.
The guard at your first office walks you to your car: "You were the only boss who said hello to me every single day."
In the ex-colleagues' chat someone suggests a mountain hike "like in 2010." You barely made it then. Now you're a legend, so there'll be photos.
right: Suggest a picnic by the river

text: The old sysadmin offers to recover your very first email account. It holds threads with your first boss and, apparently, love letters to the printer.
Vika writes: "Remember letting me leave early for a date in 2009? We've been married 14 years. Come to our anniversary."
Galya asks if she can come to your press conference. "I want to see you talk without notes now."
left: Seat her in the front row

text: Your first boss offers to co-write a chapter for your book: "The View from Above." He writes slowly, by hand only.
After the reunion Fyodor sent 400 photos. Your eyes are closed in every one. He writes: "Pick one for the book."
HR at your first company found your employment record book, which you forgot to collect 22 years ago. You have to come in person.
Timur admits he copied you in everything, even working till midnight. Now he can't sleep. What do you say?
Someone sends a video: the old office got a new coffee machine named after you. It says "good morning" in your voice.
Vika invites you to see her office. On the wall: your old photo captioned "My first mentor." You remember her with a notebook.
Zinaida offers to check your personal finances before retirement: "I know you, it's a mess." She's right.
Your first boss calls late: "Let's work together one more time in our old age." He wants to open a bakery.
The ex-colleagues' chat votes on who makes the potato salad for the reunion. Everyone picks you, because "legends can do anything."
At the reunion a former colleague you once laid off comes to shake your hand. He started his own business and is happy.
Galya hands you socks she knitted: "You're important now, but everyone's feet get cold the same way."
The old sysadmin wants to open a "museum of the first office" in the former server room. He needs your autograph on an old monitor.
The board heard about your reunions and wants to turn them into a "PR campaign." You wanted it to stay human.
You count: your first department had 12 people in 2003. Today you saw nine. Call the other three?
Your first boss brought a printout of your very first work email, covered in his red-pen comments. There are 18.
Fyodor proposes a podcast together: "Two Old-Timers at the Cooler." He's got a mic and a title.
Someone writes: "Remember how we covered for each other?" You do, and you want to thank each of them.
The board learns you left a session an hour early for the reunion and asks for a "written explanation." You haven't written one since 2003.
Your first boss asks to be introduced to your company's management: "I want to consult a bit more." He's 78 and full of energy.
Fyodor heard the board wants "reunion PR" and already gave a newspaper interview. Half of it is about his garden.
right: Ask him to clear things first

text: The CFO spots "office veterans' reunion" in the expenses and asks why the company pays.
Vika asks you to be honorary mentor to her company's first intern. The little ceremony is at 8 a.m. across town.
Your partner puts a world map and marker on the table: "Mark where you want to go when this is over." You mark only the city with a branch office.
left: Erase it and mark the sea

text: Your financial advisor says there's enough for a calm life as long as you don't buy a yacht. You weren't planning to, but now you wonder.
A travel agent offers a four-month round-the-world cruise. The board asks you to "stay reachable at least on Wednesdays." Wednesday Wi-Fi on board is extra.
The chairman asks your departure date "to plan the party." You haven't decided, but he's already ordered a cake for March.
right: Ask him not to rush you

text: You try to picture your first retired Monday. Coffee, a newspaper and… panic after 40 minutes. Need a plan?
Evening at the dacha, and you realize nobody here needs your sign-off. A call from your deputy breaks the silence.
HR asks if you'd like a "gradual" exit: four days a week, then three. Sounds like hibernation in reverse.
Your partner proposes six months by the sea after you retire. You love the sea and fear that in a week you'll start "consulting" the local fishermen.
For the first time you're packing for something other than a business trip. Your hand puts in the laptop and charger on its own. Leave them?
The CFO offers to let you keep the corporate card another year "for representation." Generous, but you wanted freedom.
Platon made you a "retirement plan": a 10-year Gantt chart with milestones like "master Nordic walking" and "let go of control."
Lyova asks if it's true that after retirement you'll spend every day with him. He's made a schedule: rockets, ice cream, rockets.
The travel agent suggests a 12-day mountain trek with tents. Your tent experience: one 2011 office retreat that ended in a hotel.
The board asks you to stay one more year "until the successor settles in." It's the third "one more year."
Your notes app: "Retirement wishes." Sleep in, learn to swim, see the northern lights. And "check email." Cross out the last one?
Your partner asks where you'll have coffee on your first morning of freedom. Options: kitchen, balcony, corner café, "the office, out of habit."
HR reminds you that you have 214 unused vacation days. Cash them out or take them before you leave?
Mom hears about your retirement and rejoices: "Finally you'll visit more!" You realize this is now your main job.
The advisor recommends "hedging" with a couple of board seats elsewhere. That's money, but also morning calls.
You're offered a 21-day stay at a country retreat. Program: walks, reading, early lights-out. Dream or boredom?
Your partner proposes planning nothing at all for your first month of freedom. Your inner manager faints.
The chairman wants your exit to be "grand": orchestra, fireworks, VIP speeches. You wanted to slip out quietly on Friday at 6 p.m.
It suddenly hits you that you don't know who you are without a title. Your new business card has just your name. Scary or wonderful?
Your daughter asks if you'll babysit on Tuesdays and Thursdays after you retire. You dreamed of freedom, and of grandkids too.
You skipped the alarm on day one of vacation. Your internal clock woke you at 5:57. Lie in or get up?
right: Get up and enjoy the morning

text: The travel agent pitches a "career tour": every city you went to on business. You only ever saw the hotels.
Your partner found a couples' course: "Life After Career." First assignment: talk about anything except work every evening.
Platon asks whether to shut off your work email on your last day or a month later "for smoothness."
The board wants you to sign a two-year "no consulting for competitors" clause. You weren't going to, but competitors are already calling.
Evening. You scroll through retired ex-colleagues' trip photos: mountains, fishing, grandkids. You want that and fear it at once.
The advisor suggests investing in a seaside cottage "while prices are low." The cottage needs repairs; you need peace.
Staff are collecting for your farewell gift and secretly ask your partner what you dream of. The answer: "Silence."
right: Ask them not to spend money

text: Your son suggests a week-long fishing trip together, "like you promised when I was little." You did. Many times.
For the first time you read a novel in the morning instead of market news. Ten minutes in your hand reaches for your phone "to check the rates."
The chairman offers you an "honorary office" after you leave. The plaque's ready. You fear you'll come in every day.
right: Take it, once a month max

text: Your partner asks what you fear most about leaving. Honestly: "That nobody will call." Your partner promises to call.
HR sent an exit survey. Question 7: "What would you change about the company?" You've been writing for two hours.
Lyova drew your "retirement office": hammock, fishing rod, rocket and cat. Caption: "Nobody works here anymore." Fridge or old office?
At the dacha you sleep 10 hours for the first time in a year. The neighbor asks: "Are you ill?" Explain it's just rest?
The chairman wants to mint a commemorative coin for your departure. Run of 100. You think it's overkill.
right: Agree and give them to staff

text: The advisor asks if you'd like to start a charitable foundation. Lovely, but it's another job, office and board.
Your to-do list for day one of freedom has 23 items. It looks like you're working again.
A retirees' hiking club invites you on a kayak trip. Average age: 71. Pace: "fast."
The board wants you to record a "video for posterity" for employees 20 years from now. What do you tell the people of 2046?
Your partner wants a dinner at home for your closest people on your last day. The board wants a 300-guest banquet the same night.
Oleg asks if he can call you after you leave "only in emergencies." For Oleg, a typo in a report is an emergency.
left: Give him a list of real emergencies

text: You're planning rest like a quarterly budget: spreadsheet, scenarios, risks. Maybe rest starts with ditching the spreadsheet?
The travel agent calls back at 9:30 p.m.: "Last seat on the northern lights tour, decide now." It's the week of the annual meeting.
The receptionist asks what to do with your partners' gifts: 46 figurines, 12 vases and a bust of an unknown man.
The board suggests a "farewell tour of branches": 9 cities in 12 days. You suggest video calls. The board calls that "disrespectful."
At 8 a.m. the supermarket cashier recognizes you: "Is it true you don't work Fridays?" The line behind you clearly wants the answer.
Marketing released a sticker pack of your face. The most popular one: "Could've been an email." People use it to reply to your meeting invites.
A fan sent you a 12-page handwritten analysis of your career. At the end: "a few words back, please."
In the elevator a stranger rehearses a pitch and realizes at the end he's pitching to you. Eighteen floors to go.
right: Get off at the next floor

text: Security reports a fake account of you giving investment advice online. It has more followers than you do.
right: Joke about it on your account

text: The innovation team built a digital twin of you to answer interns' questions. It's faster and kinder than you.
The board commissioned an oil portrait of you for the lobby. The artist wants you to sit two hours every morning for a week. You can't sit still.
The cafeteria launched "The Legend's Plate": buckwheat and a cutlet, like you ate for 20 years. Now everyone orders it and the cooks can't keep up.
Your neighbor asks you to sign books for his mother-in-law, mother, sister and two coworkers. Five books, and you're in slippers.
The intranet launched a "Legend Advises" column signed with your name. One tip you never gave: "Sleep 4 hours a night."
right: Ask them to quietly remove it

text: The city business museum wants your old work chair for an exhibit. You're sitting on it right now.
The cabbie recognized you and pitched his business idea the whole ride. You've arrived, but he offers "one more lap."
right: Wish him luck and get out

text: Clients insist you attend their meetings in person: "We buy from the legend." Salespeople are hurt, and sales are up.
A rival firm runs an ad: "Work with us: like the legend's company, minus the legend." Your staff laugh; the board doesn't.
You notice restaurants bring you free dessert. Nice, but you've been cutting back on sweets for three weeks.
A business school wants to name a lecture hall after you. It's the very room where you once failed an exam.
Platon shows you a sack of fan mail. One's from a boy: "I want to be like you but I don't know what your job is."
You suddenly have a fan club. They meet Friday night and invite you "for five minutes at least."
The company lot now has a "Legend Only" space. You arrive by bike; the sales director's car is parked there.
A recruitment agency uses your photo: "We found the legend." They never found you.
A channel is making a show "inspired by your life." The actor playing you jumps out of a helicopter every episode.
The café by the office named a drink after you: "The Legend: double espresso with oat milk." You drink tea.
The board wants a life-size cardboard cutout of you in the lobby. People can "hug it for photos."
Tonight you got 80 birthday wishes. Your birthday is six months away; someone botched the directory.
At the airport the crew asks for a photo. You're late for boarding, but the pilot says: "We won't leave without you."
Misha started "legend tours" for newcomers: your desk, your mug, your favorite window corner. One is passing you right now.
right: Ask for no tours during work hours

text: You read an online article about yourself and believed in your own genius for 20 minutes. Back to earth?
The barista recognizes you and draws your portrait in the foam. You can't bring yourself to drink it. The meeting's in 5 minutes.
left: Snap a photo and drink it

text: The new doorman doesn't know you and demands a pass. He's the first person all year not to recognize you. You're almost happy.
left: Show your pass with a smile

text: Marketing released a board game, "Office Legend." Your piece is a coffee mug. The family plays and you're losing as yourself.
Security says a blogger is camped at the entrance to "film the legend's reaction to his startup." He has a sign.
A bookstore shelved your book under "Fantasy." The clerk swears it sells better there.
Lyova says kids at school asked if his grandparent is "that meme." He's proud but a bit embarrassed.
The chairman forwards 200 emails from people who "just want to meet the legend." He writes: "Maybe an open house day?"
The lawyer says someone trademarked "Survive till Friday" and sells T-shirts. Sue?
The fan club held a look-alike contest. The winner is so convincing your cat went to him. Ask him to stand in for you at a banquet?
You notice you've started speaking in quotes from your own book. At home they give you funny looks. Stop?
The training team runs a quiz: "How well do you know the legend?" You join incognito and come fourth.
Neighbors posted a note in the building: "Please don't disturb the legend after 8 p.m." Awkward, but peaceful.
Lisa offers to run your blog to "bring the legend closer to people." Her first proposed post: your breakfast.
The press office asks you to stop eating at the ordinary café: "It hurts your image." It has the best soup in town.
right: Order the soup to the office

text: Platon asks whether to reply to a fan who wants to name her daughter after you. Your name is rather unusual.
The board realizes you get more invites than all board members combined. Someone's sulking. Share the invites?
Sales jumped after your interview. The team wants one every week. "It's a KPI."
Your partner is tired of people coming up to you every ten minutes at restaurants. Suggests dining at home or in another city.
IT says your name was used in a phishing email: "The legend urgently asks for a transfer." Three staff nearly fell for it.
The business museum wants to display a clay bust of you made by a kids' art studio. Not very accurate, but very earnest.
The chairman calls in the evening: in "Most Recognizable Business Faces" you're #1, and he's #42. His congratulations are very dry.
The CFO notes security costs tripled because of your fame. He suggests you "appear at the office less."
A major shareholder asks for an autograph for his grandson right in the middle of the vote. Everyone's watching.
right: Ask him to wait for the break

text: You're getting a "Contribution to Business" award. The ceremony is Friday at 7 p.m., same as your granddaughter's birthday.
right: Pop into the ceremony for 20 min

text: You're on the jury of a startup contest. One finalist is your former mentee Danya. Recuse yourself?
Your shelf has 23 award statuettes. Nobody dusts them and tossing them feels wrong. What to do?
A young founder asks you to be an advisor "for equity." His app reminds you to drink water. Every four minutes.
The chairman wants to nominate you for an international award. You'd fill out a 40-page form about yourself.
At the award ceremony the emcee mixed you up with another winner and read your bio with someone else's details. The hall applauds.
A venture fund invites you to be a partner: "Three meetings a week and a little magic." Your magic ran out last quarter.
A startup asks you to come to demo day "just to stand nearby." Your presence will raise their valuation. You know nothing about the product.
The committee wants a 90-second speech. You've written nine minutes, all thank-yous. Whom do you cut?
left: Thank the team in one line

text: Another company invites you onto its board. Your current board calls it "betrayal with aggravating circumstances."
An accelerator asks you to run 30 mentoring sessions in two days. Fifteen minutes each, no breaks.
Your partner asks why you need another award when at the last ceremony you dreamed of pajamas all night.
A founder sends a 90-slide deck at 6:30 a.m.: "Your thoughts by 9." Slide 1: your photo labeled "our future advisor."
A university is giving you an honorary doctorate. Gown, cap and a speech in Latin. Your Latin ends at "carpe."
You won "Leader of the Decade" and felt only tired. Maybe that's a sign?
An investor friend asks you to "take a look at a company" at 8 a.m. on site. It's a bakery, and there's a croissant in it for you.
You're the only juror who read all 300 entries. The others want "a quick summary" from you.
A founder texts at 11 p.m.: "Thanks for the advice! We did the opposite and tripled." Ouch, and yay.
An industry association wants to elect you chair. Meetings on Thursdays, and Thursday is ceramics day.
At the award ceremony the photographer wants a "legendary" smile. You smile as usual. He's unhappy.
Lyova asks if he can take your crystal award to the sandbox "as a bucket." It does look very much like a bucket.
A charity asks you to be a trustee. Honorable, with four meetings a year. In the morning.
The chairman wants the company logo on all your awards. Half are for the choir and pumpkins.
A startup named its product after you without asking. It's a smart mousetrap.
Platon asks whether to accept a jury seat for "Best Office Kitchen." You once filed a complaint about your first office kitchen.
A founder asks: "How much to just mention us now and then?" The sum is substantial.
The committee asks for last year's statuette back "to repaint it." You use it as a plant stand.
right: Buy a new stand, then return it

text: A business school wants to study your career as a case. There'll be a chapter on "Mistakes." They wrote it without you.
A startup invites you to a 2 p.m. meeting at a 12th-floor coworking space. The elevator's broken. The topic: "healthy lifestyle."
right: Invite them down to a café

text: You notice you enjoy giving awards to young people more than receiving them. Start your own prize?
The chairman asks you to represent the company at an international expo. A week at a booth, smiling.
An angel investor friend wants you in on a soup-by-drone startup. The soup spilled twice in testing.
Your partner suggests hanging all your certificates in the bathroom: "Everyone will see them there." Joke or not, it's unclear.
A trade magazine wants a weekly column. Pays little, but everyone reads it.
A former rival suggests you co-present an award to young entrepreneurs. You haven't spoken in twenty years.
A founder sends you a box of his protein bars in "office coffee" flavor. He wants a review.
The board wants you to accept "Employer of the Year" personally. You think the HR team deserves it.
right: Go and thank them on stage

text: An accelerator wants your "secret ingredient for success" for a booklet. Honest answer: "Sleep enough and don't argue with accounting."
The committee wants you presenting till midnight: "Guests will leave without you." You promised your partner you'd be home at 10.
A founder asks you to attend his wedding "as a lucky charm." You've met once.
A big corporation offers you a board seat with a huge salary. Fifteen hours a week, which is all your future freedom.
For the first time you turned down an award, because it's fishing day with your son. You don't regret it one bit.
The chairman forwards an offer to be the "face" of an industry expo: a 10-by-20-meter banner photo.
A startup asks you to sit in on a meeting and "just observe." Twenty minutes in they're fighting and everyone looks at you.
Platon reports: "You've been nominated for Calmest Leader." You laugh so loud the neighbors bang on the radiator.
A young founder gives an ultimatum: "If you won't advise us, we'll shut down." You see manipulation in it.
The jury can't pick a winner: two projects are tied. Everyone looks to you for the deciding vote.
Your partner proposes a rule: every new award earns a day off. That's 11 days owed to you this year.
Danya won the startup contest and thanks you longer than his investors in his speech. The investors exchange looks.
right: Go up and hand it to the investors

text: The committee sent an invoice for the "laureate package": photos, video and a head-table seat. Turns out you pay for the award.
Your new phone's screen-time report: you average 6 hours a day in email. It suggests a 2-hour limit. Dare?
You've talked for 30 minutes on a board video call while everyone waves: you're muted. Repeat everything?
At 10 p.m. your smart speaker says: "You have 8 meetings tomorrow. Maybe go to bed early?" Even the speaker is worried.
right: Ask it to read the agenda

text: Your grandson made you a social media account and overnight you have 40,000 followers. Everyone awaits the first post.
IT built a chatbot that answers staff questions with your quotes. It's already advised "go home early" three times.
Your laptop demands an update now, and your webinar for 5,000 starts in 10 minutes. The update takes 40.
You need to e-sign 120 documents. The token's gone missing; last seen in the pocket of an old jacket.
IT wants you to switch from your paper planner to a digital one. Yours holds 30 years of wisdom and tea stains.
Your granddaughter taught you video filters. You accidentally joined a partners' call as a kitten.
1,200 unread emails. Your assistant suggests declaring "email bankruptcy": archive everything and start fresh.
An AI wrote your holiday message to staff. It's lovely, but mentions "our beloved dolphins."
You set your messenger status to "Do not disturb." A minute later: "Sorry to disturb you." Answer?
Your watch buzzes: "You've been sitting 3 hours. Stand up!" You're in a board meeting; standing now looks like a protest.
You were mistakenly added to the "Surprise for the Legend" chat. They're discussing your farewell gift.
Your son set up a smart home. Now lights switch off at 11 p.m. and a lullaby plays. Override it?
IT wants a new password: 16 characters, caps, numbers, symbols. You're used to "Friday1."
Video call with a branch. Half have cameras off, and one's asleep. Address it?
You accidentally sent the whole holding company "Buy milk and cat food." 300 people replied "Bought it!"
An AI generated your press release portrait. You have six fingers and a very confident gaze.
IT wants to block your work email on your phone after 8 p.m. It was your idea for the staff.
Your voice note to a mentee turned into a 12-minute lecture. It sent. Delete it or let him listen?
The new office printer prints from phones, by voice and "by mood." It prints your report in pink.
Your post "Leaving work at 5 today" got a million views. Comments split between "inspiring" and "easy for you to say."
Your laptop notices you typing at 11:30 p.m. and suggests "sleep mode." First for the screen, then for you.
For the first time in a year you left home without your phone. An hour ago. A strange feeling: anxiety or freedom.
Marketing wants a live stream every Friday at 5 p.m., "Friday Talk with the Legend." At 5 you go home.
Your daughter shows you how to set an auto-reply: "Gone fishing, back Monday." You'd like to set it for life.
The intranet wants an "Ask the Legend" button. Questions from 12,000 employees would come to you.
On a video call you notice you've had your granddaughter's hair clip on for 20 minutes.
Your partner suggests a "digital sabbath," 24 hours screen-free. You agree and an hour later check the weather on the smart fridge.
IT offers to let you keep your work laptop when you leave. It holds your whole life, including a "Do Not Open" folder.
You hit "Reply all" on a congratulations email to someone you don't know. Now everyone replies "Thanks from the whole team!"
Lyova's teaching you an online game. Players in chat recognize you and ask for career advice. He's horrified.
A 6 a.m. call with overseas partners. You're in a blazer and pajama pants. The camera shows only the top. For now.
IT wants to record your voice so an AI can narrate your audiobook and wish staff happy birthday. Forever.
At 11:50 p.m. your successor texts: "Still up?" You are, but you'd rather not be.
IT issued face-recognition passes. The turnstile won't recognize you: you're without glasses and in a good mood.
You accidentally liked a rival's post. Media are already writing about a "merger."
