Scrolling, you see former colleagues on vacation. You compare and feel a little envious. What to do?
You're in 47 work chats. In one, your last message dates from 2019: "OK."
IT asks whether to migrate your 25-year email archive to the new system. It's bigger than the rest of the company.
Your granddaughter video-calls to show a drawing, right in the middle of your online lecture. Her call pops up on screen.
right: Show the drawing to the audience

text: Morning inbox: 15 emails marked "URGENT!!!" Only one is truly urgent, and it has no exclamation marks.
You reacted with a heart to a message about an employee's layoff. You meant the sad face.
Your son showed you how to mute notifications. For the first time in 20 years you eat dinner without buzzing in your pocket.
The CFO wants approval for 300 tablets "like the legend's." Yours is a kids' tablet with your grandson's stickers.
The chairman wants a new video-meeting system that shows who talks most. You top the minutes.
The board emails at 10:40 p.m. marked "for the morning." You see it at 10:41. When is "morning," exactly?
The intranet poll to name a new meeting room: your name is leading; second place is "The Closet."
IT asks you to take mandatory cybersecurity training: 4 hours plus a test. You're the last one in the company who hasn't.
An agency offers a huge fee to front a credit card "for those surviving till Friday." You're against living on debt till Friday.
The CFO proposes a farewell bonus equal to the interns' annual budget. The interns don't know.
You realize your book credits you with an idea a former colleague actually proposed. It's already on sale.
A business partner sent you an expensive watch "in memory of our cooperation." Company rules forbid such gifts.
Platon confesses he wrote half your social posts. Followers praise your "lively style."
Your neighbor asks you to slip his son into an internship "through the back door." He once fixed your car in a blizzard.
left: Point him to the open contest

text: A reporter wants an "investigative interview" about your former rival. You know unflattering things, but it was long ago.
Your advisor suggests investing savings in a fund "everyone's talking about." Mostly the ads are talking.
Your son asks for a big loan for his startup. You believe in him, not in the startup.
right: Ask for a business plan first

text: The board offers to keep paying you a year "for consultations" that may never happen.
The press office wants to say you personally donated a million to a school. The company did; you only cut the ribbon.
A former report writes: "You were unfair in my 2015 review." You reread it; he's right.
The publisher wants to edit the chapter about your mistake so "circumstances" are to blame.
Sales asks you to call a client and promise what the company can't deliver. "You're a legend, they'll believe you."
A foundation asks you to auction personal items. Lot #1: your old mug, which Timur still has.
A rival wants to buy your book in bulk for its staff. Your publisher's delighted; your board is suspicious.
The HR director asks you to sign a reference she wrote for an ex-employee. It's all glowing; you remember otherwise.
You promised interns "my door is always open," yet for three months your secretary has turned them away "due to your schedule."
A shareholder calls: "Just whisper what's coming at the board. Only to me." He's an old friend.
Lisa overheard about layoffs and asks you directly: "Will I be let go?" You know, but you can't say.
Your partner proposes giving half the book royalties to charity. You'd hoped they'd fund a seaside trip.
right: A quarter to charity, rest for the sea

text: The chairman asks you not to mention a failed project in your farewell speech. It was his idea.
A sponsor will fund your charity program if you publicly say you use their bank. You don't.
right: Open an account and use it

text: Your daughter finds an error in your book: you wrote you never missed her school concerts. You missed four.
The CFO suggests "optimizing" your travel expenses: log your seaside vacation as a "conference."
Misha found an error in your famous talk: revenue was doubled. The video has 2 million views.
You got a full fee for a talk that was cut from 40 to 7 minutes. The organizer did the cutting. Return some?
Fyodor asks you to co-sign a loan for a tractor. His garden is 600 square meters.
The lawyer asks whether the book should name real deal amounts. Readers love it; partners won't.
Sonya asks for a grant recommendation. Her project is good, but an old friend of yours is on the jury.
A partner offers a personal bonus if you "nudge" the board toward a deal. The deal's decent, but the bonus is a bribe.
HR proposes lifetime family health insurance in your exit package, funded by cutting middle managers' bonuses.
Lyova found your old diaries: did you really dream of "getting rich and bossing everyone around" at 25? You did.
You promised a charity a free masterclass. The same day there's a big-money paid lecture.
The board wants to announce you're leaving "to spend time with family." True, but it sounds like a cliché.
You realize you're still angry at someone who let you down 15 years ago. It drains you. Let it go?
Platon suggests charging for interviews "like all legends do." You've always given them free.
A major shareholder wants his nephew on the foundation board. The nephew is sweet but knows only the word "foundation."
Your partner found your draft will in your phone notes, right next to the shopping list. Time for a grown-up talk?
A journalist wants comment on rumors your successor "can't do anything." His rival is spreading them.
The CFO asks you to sign a report listing last year's taxi costs as "strategic investments."
Your mentees pooled money for a farewell gift and ask what you want. You'd rather they spend it on themselves.
A founder offers equity "for your name on the website." It could be millions, or nothing.
HR offers you an "employer brand ambassador" stipend. You're already an ambassador for free.
You tally the years spent in meetings that could've been emails: 3.5 years. Do something about it?
The chairman asks you to leave "quietly," no interviews, so as not to upstage new leadership.
You promised to run a charity 10 km for every million the foundation raised. It raised four million.
You stayed up late checking whether the foundation overpays rent. You found savings of about three dollars. Worth the evening?
left: Go to bed, no more checks

text: Platon asks if he can moonlight on weekends helping other "legends." You're jealous but you understand.
right: Ask him to wait till you leave

text: The advisor pitches "passive income": short-term rentals. Which means greeting guests at 3 a.m.
Alarm at 6 a.m., but you got to bed at 1:30 after a flight. Podcast recording at 10 can't be moved. Sleep another hour?
right: Get up and go for a run

text: The office opened a nap room with beanbags. You want 15 minutes, but fear staff will see "the legend on a beanbag."
9 p.m. For the third day in a row you're eating dinner standing at the fridge. Sit at the table, at least tonight?
The elevator's broken and your office is on floor 14. You've long promised yourself to "move more." The board meets in 15 minutes.
right: Hold the meeting in the lobby

text: Lunch break. They bring a container to your desk so you "don't waste time." You miss eating in the canteen with people.
You've run a bubble bath for the first time in five years. The phone on the edge buzzes: the chairman.
A personal trainer, a gift from staff for your anniversary, waits at 7 a.m. You've never gone, and the voucher expires Friday.
Platon noticed you haven't had water all day and put a pitcher on your desk with a reminder every 30 minutes. It'll derail meetings, of course.
Your partner proposes a 30-minute walk together every evening. Every evening you remember "one urgent email."
Vacation's begun, but you woke at 5:58 and opened email "for a minute." It's 9:00 and you're still in it.
left: Close it, go to the beach

text: A massage chair in the lobby has a queue. Staff offer to let you skip it "as the legend."
For the first time in years you're so tired you can't recall what day it is. Cancel tomorrow's meetings?
By 10 a.m. you're on your fifth coffee. Your hands are a bit shaky. Switch to tea?
Misha brings you a snack: "You skipped lunch, I saw." It's carrot sticks and hummus. You dreamed of a pastry.
You went to bed at 10:30 as promised. At 11:15 your brain produces a brilliant board idea. Get up and write it down?
left: Jot it on your phone in the dark

text: Gorgeous weather; you decide to walk to work: 50 minutes through the park. But there's a call at 9.
HR launched a 10,000-steps challenge. You top the leaderboard because you pace nervously in meetings with your phone in pocket.
At 9 p.m. the cat lies on your chest and purrs. Getting up would be betrayal. Thirty emails await.
You can't remember the last time you looked out the window for no reason. It's snowing. Five minutes?
The meeting's in its third hour. You suggest standing to speed it up. Half the room glares.
You came to the dacha for the weekend and fell asleep in the hammock at 5 p.m. You woke at 9. Neighbors were worried.
Platon added "15 minutes of nothing" to your calendar three times daily. Staff ask what those important meetings are.
The new office has treadmill desks. You try one and accidentally email "asdfgh" to the chairman.
Your partner warns: fall asleep with the laptop on your lap once more and it moves to the balcony. You're nodding off again.
Routine checkup. The doctor asks how many hours you sleep. You say "enough," and she looks over her glasses.
You catch yourself holding your breath while reading board emails. Maybe try breathing?
For the first time in a month you cooked dinner yourself. It took ages and tasted great. Meeting at 7 a.m. Do the dishes now or in the morning?
You biked to work and feel 20 years younger. But in the elevator everyone stares at the clip on your trouser leg.
You ordered lunch for 1 p.m., but the meeting's dragging. Your lunch is cooling and your stomach rumbles so all can hear.
You promised not to work on Sundays. It's Sunday, 8 p.m., and you're opening "just tomorrow's calendar."
Online morning yoga: the instructor wants you to "feel your connection to the earth." You feel the rug and doubt.
On vacation. The board sends a "quick question" that'll take two hours to answer. The beach is right there.
Your partner suggests the sauna with friends on Saturday. You haven't been in 10 years and aren't sure you remember how to relax there.
Monday morning. You set an auto-reply: "On Mondays I don't answer before 11." It's an experiment. The board probably won't like it.
Colleagues invite you for a lunchtime walk around the block. You usually eat at your desk reading reports.
Your partner set a "Bedtime" alarm for 10 p.m. It rings mid-email to the board.
You woke with a plan: no email for 30 minutes after waking. It's been 15 and your hand is twitching.
Everyone in the meeting is exhausted. You propose cancelling the second half so everyone can breathe till tomorrow. The board's dialed in and listening.
You found a show that truly relaxes you: village gardening. It has 14 seasons.
HR proposes "meeting-free Fridays" for everyone. The board asks your view. You've dreamed of this for 20 years.
Platon says you have five back-to-back meetings and asks to trim each by 5 minutes so you can "stand up at least once."
You cancelled an evening meeting and feel guilty, though you're on the balcony with tea and a sunset. Guilt or sunset?
First sunny morning of spring. You want breakfast on a café terrace; your calendar says investor breakfast in a windowless room.
You've learned front crawl and want to swim at lunch three times a week. That means 90 minutes out of the office.
For the first time in years you put on music and dance in the kitchen. Neighbors see you through the window and wave.
You make your day plan and realize there isn't a minute for yourself. Strike one meeting?
Staff give you a pool pass "so you finally rest." Underneath: "And don't call us from the pool."
Your partner turns off your phone and hides it in the closet. "Till morning." You fume, then sleep 9 hours.
Sonya sees you rubbing your eyes and offers to run your next meeting: "I've got it, you take a nap."
The team agreed in chat not to message you after 7 p.m. "for your own good." You feel cared for and a tiny bit offended.
right: Ask them to write if it matters

text: You're invited to teach "Career Without Burnout" to master's students. Classes are Mondays at 8:30. You're an owl, and Monday's the enemy.
A student raises a hand: "What if I don't want to be a legend, just to live normally?" The class applauds.
Students invite you to their dorm for "tea with the legend." The tea turns out to be instant noodles for 40.
A school asks you to explain "how an office works" in tech class. The kids expect robots; you have a slideshow about accounting.
The dean asks you to grade 60 term papers by Friday. "You're an honorary professor, it's just a formality."
A student writes at 10 p.m.: "Your lecture changed my life, I quit law school for ceramics." Her mother will probably call you.
right: Suggest she talk to her parents

text: A young entrepreneurs' club wants you as an "investor" in their lemonade business: about five dollars and one consultation.
The rector wants a scholarship in your name, funded from your personal money.
Students sent a parody of your talk. The impersonator holds a mug and says "Could've been an email." Funny and spot-on.
right: Ask them not to post it

text: A high-school senior writes: "What should I study to be like you?" You studied engineering and never worked a day as an engineer.
A seminar student argues offices will soon vanish. You've spent 40 years in them.
Grading student essays, you see your lectures quoted incorrectly but beautifully. Correct them?
The university asks you to speak at graduation, Saturday 9 a.m. You promised your grandson backyard soccer at 9 a.m. Saturday.
A PhD student is writing a dissertation on your management style and wants a 6-hour interview. Your style is short meetings.
Students hold a quiz in your honor. "How many cups of coffee does the legend drink a day?" Correct answer: zero. Everyone loses.
You're at a school for a "lesson in success." A first-grader asks: "Do you have a dog?" That's all he cares about.
The department wants an exam for your course. You wanted none: "How can you teach stress-free living with stress?"
A former student writes ten years later: "I'm a director now and banned meetings after 5 p.m. Thank you!"
The student council wants your advice on organizing a festival. Budget: zero. Expectations: world-forum level.
The rector offers you an office "to work with students." That's a second job, and you're leaving the first to rest.
Students sent a thank-you video, each saying what you taught them. Half say: "Go home on time."
You're on the jury of a school economics olympiad. The problems are so hard you're still solving them at lunch.
A young lecturer asks you to sit in and give feedback. He's nervous, the students too: "The legend's in the room."
You realize the students taught you more than you taught them: the word "cringe," a note-taking app, and that you don't have to hurry.
Your grandson's kindergarten invites you to Career Day. Other parents: a firefighter and a pastry chef. You: "a legend."
left: Bring a cake from the chef

text: The university wants to record your course and sell it online. Money for them, fame for you, work also for you.
A student asks for an internship at your company. You barely work there now and can't promise anything.
A literature teacher assigns your book as extra reading. Ninth-graders write essays: "Why the Legend Got Tired."
A student team wants a post-mortem of their failed startup. They're expecting praise; it was an objective flop.
The PhD student calls again at 9:30 p.m.: "One more tiny question for the dissertation." It's the twentieth.
The dean begs you for a guest lecture today at 11, the lecturer is ill. You have yoga at 11.
A student asks if an introvert can become a leader. You're an introvert who played extrovert for 30 years.
Lyova joins your online lecture and asks in chat as "Rocket3000": "When are you coming home?"
The student paper calls you "business's top boomer." You can't tell if it's a compliment.
The university wants your archive of work notebooks. Forty of them, one with your 1999 grocery list.
Students throw you a farewell lecture with a surprise: a song about Friday. Badly sung, but from the heart.
A schoolboy interviewing you for a project asks: "How much do you earn?" His teacher turns pale.
The rector invites you onto the university's board of trustees. Four meetings a year, eight banquets.
You count: this year you gave students more advice than your own kids in ten. An uncomfortable discovery.
Schoolkids want to "rent" you for the fair as a living attraction. Payment: tickets to the school play.
A student asks how to balance study, work and sport. Honestly, you didn't balance them, you took turns.
Students invite you to an all-night hackathon. Pizza and "the legend live until dawn." You sleep at 11.
You're offered the face of the university's ad campaign: you in a college hoodie with a backpack.
The dean finds you gave everyone top marks. "That's against the rules." You think everyone tried hard.
A former student sends a photo: his daughter reading your book. Caption: "Learning to leave at 6 from an early age."
The PhD student defends his dissertation about you and invites you. The committee asks questions about you… to you.
At 8 p.m. a student sends her first résumé. Under "Skills": "knows how to rest, as the legend taught."
The chairman is unhappy: you lecture at the university on Mondays, while the board expects you at 9 on Mondays.
The CFO asks why your university lecture was billed to the company as "corporate training." Good question.
You stayed up till midnight on a presentation for schoolkids. The topic: why sleep matters.
Your last week. Packing your office, you find 14 mugs, 3 umbrellas and a tie you've never seen. What do you take?
left: Just the photos and the cactus

text: Staff are secretly planning your farewell, labeled "Budget meeting" in your calendar. You nearly declined.
At your farewell you're asked for a speech. You prepared three pages, but you spot Galya, Fyodor and Timur and want to say it differently.
Last week, and your successor wants a "full handover day" on Saturday. Saturday's promised to family.
Platon's list: 87 people want a "last one-on-one." Five working days left.
The evening before your first month-long vacation in ten years. You leave the office, the guard waves, the cooler gurgles, lights go out behind you on the sensor. Look back?
The chairman proposes a "last strategy session," all day. You suspect it's mostly his nostalgia session.
HR asks you to return your pass, laptop and "the office key unchanged since 1998." You lost it long ago.
At the farewell party Fyodor demands "the famous ficus dance." Someone has already brought the ficus.
Your desk is buried in cards. One says: "Thanks for teaching me to say no. No, I won't come to your farewell."
The receptionist starts a "wishes book" in the lobby. In two hours 200 people sign it; someone draws you with wings.
right: Save it for day one of rest

text: Your partner comes to the farewell and sees hundreds hug you. At home that night: "Now you're ours."
Your successor asks for a note on the desk "like presidents do." You'll write one word, but which?
Marketing's shooting a farewell video and wants you to walk the office one last time "slowly, with warmth in your eyes." Take twelve.
At the farewell Lyova climbs on stage and says into the mic: "Now Grandma/Grandpa is mine!" A standing ovation.
Your mentees show up at 7:30 with breakfast "for one last unscheduled chat." Pancakes that Danya made all night.
The lawyer brings a 40-page termination-of-authority agreement. The last page has a signature line and a smiley from the lawyer.
Galya hands you the key to the storeroom where you once hid from management. "As a keepsake, and just in case."
The board asks you to sign one "last" order: renaming your office "The Legend's Office."
Accounting needs all your expense reports closed before you go. You have three from the past two years and no receipts.
Last evening. You sit in your chair in the empty office and realize you won't miss the chair. The people, you will.
Staff line the hallway in a "guard of honor," applauding. Walk through fast or greet each one?
Timur brings back the famous mug to return it ceremonially. But without it he's afraid of big meetings.
The farewell's host wants "a last toast from the legend" at 11:30 p.m. You meant to leave at 10, as you taught everyone.
Platon clears every meeting after Friday. Your calendar goes white. You gaze at it like fresh snow.
IT locks your account at 6 p.m. Friday. At 5:55 you remember you haven't sent one last email.
The family greets you with a banner: "Welcome to life." The kitchen smells of pie. Your phone rings: the board.
First morning of your long vacation. You wake at 6 with no idea what to do. The cat stares expectantly.
left: Feed the cat, back to bed

text: The office calls you on vacation: "Where's the supplier contract? Only you know." You do.
Mentees started a "Retired Legend" chat to ask advice now and then. You're the admin. Already 112 messages.
The box from the office has sat in the hallway for a week. Unpack it, or take it to the dacha and forget it?
Your successor sends a photo: he hung your portrait in the meeting room. "So you can glare when I mess up."
left: Ask him to take it down

text: Your partner asks how your first laptop-free vacation day went. Honestly: "Strange. Good. Strangely good."
A week into your vacation, the chairman calls "just to see how you are." A minute later he's asking about a deal.
For the first time you go grocery shopping on a weekday at 11. It's empty, quiet, smells of bread. Is this freedom?
left: Buy a loaf and enjoy it
right: Call the office from the store

text: Fyodor writes: "So, free bird, fishing on Thursday?" A regular working Thursday. You can!
You turned off every alarm forever. At 7 your visiting grandson wakes you. He's the new alarm.
The board asks you to interrupt your vacation for the quarterly meeting: "Just an hour, as an honored guest." You want to and don't.
Evening, week two of vacation. On the balcony you realize you didn't think about work once all day.
For the first time in a month your successor doesn't call. You miss it and feel a little slighted. Call him?
A neighbor wants you on the building committee. "You know how to lead." You wanted to rest, not lead.
The family proposes a new tradition: Friday night pizza and a movie. Friday sounds completely different now.
For the first time you wake not with "what must I do today" but "what do I want today." Unfamiliar.
The office writes to you on vacation: "We started meeting-free Fridays, like you dreamed." You smile at the message.
Your partner proposes celebrating a month of vacation. How? "By doing nothing together."
Your first department's old crew sends an evening video: they've gathered at the cooler, raising water cups to your freedom.
At 9 p.m., while you're on vacation, the CFO calls: "One last question on the report, honestly the last." It's the fourth "last."
The board sends a farewell gift: a rocking chair engraved "Rest. We've got this." You're not sure they do.
On your last day Sonya asks: "Tell me one thing I should remember forever." The whole department freezes to listen.
On your last morning the guard waves you through without a pass: "Today you walk in like it's home."
At the stand-up everyone falls silent and looks at you: "Whatever the legend says." You want them to decide. Stay pointedly quiet?
Sales hung your portrait above the register as a mascot. Sales rose 3%. The board wants portraits in every branch.
left: Talk the board out of it

text: In the evening a new cleaner asks you to lift your feet so she can mop under the desk. She doesn't know who you are, and that's lovely.
Interns took the room you booked: "We thought the legend doesn't use tiny rooms."
A sign in the kitchen: "The legend's mug. Do not wash: historic patina." It hasn't been washed in six months.
Evening meeting. You say: "Let's wrap by six." Everyone laughs, thinking it's a joke.
Procurement asks which pens to order for you. You've used one pen you found at a 1996 conference for 30 years.
Misha asks if he can take your seat in the meeting while you stand by the window. The board watches with interest.
The guard warns the alarm goes on at 8 p.m. and asks you to leave. You're finishing an email to the board.
You decide to work in the open space for a week "like everyone." In the first hour 23 people drop by "for a sec."
The company counselor asks you to tell staff about your burnout. It's honest, but the board fears for your image.
At 7 p.m. the coffee machine displays: "Legend, enough coffee for today." Your mentees reprogrammed it.
Platon asks if he can cancel a meeting "just because you're tired." The first such request in your whole career.
The board wants you to sign a "Legend's Code" for newcomers: 50 rules. Rule 1: "Always smile."
In the evening someone posts: "The legend's still here?! So we can't leave either?" You are still here.
The floor printer churns out 300 pages of your own book; someone sent it by mistake. A line of colleagues grows.
The CFO admits he can't read your handwriting on the approved budget. It says either "yes" or "fish."
8:30 p.m. You're alone in the office and realize you're the "boss who never leaves" you mocked at 25.
A courier brings a huge fruit basket from partners: "For the legend and team." At 8 a.m. the team isn't in yet.
A fire drill. Everyone's out but they're looking for you because "the legend never leaves their post." You were just in the restroom.
A guy from the company next door knocks at 7:30 p.m.: "Your light's on. You're always here. Got a charger?"
IT's replacing monitors. You get a giant curved one, "fit for a legend." All you see is your reflection.
The HR director wants a "Legend Day" when everyone wears your signature blue shirt. You don't have a signature shirt.
Lisa's staying late because "you're still here." You're staying late because "Lisa's still here."
A display at reception reads: "The legend is in the office today." The receptionist switches it on whenever you walk in.
Oleg asks you to attend his big meeting "for weight." You'd sit silently for two hours.
The guard confesses he bets: if you leave before 7, tomorrow will be sunny. Yesterday it poured.
The canteen gives you free coffee "because legend." Everyone behind you pays. Awkward.
A salesperson asks you to talk to a difficult client who "only wants the legend." The client wants 40% off.
You leave at 6 p.m. and feel ashamed, though you taught everyone not to. Walk proudly past the open space?
The training team asks you to run a morning workshop on "How to Say No." You've already said yes to three other workshops.
The chairman wants a "traditional speech" from you at every company celebration. There are 11 a year.
Your mentees host an "uncensored Q&A night." First question: "Have you ever cried at work?"
At the morning meeting everyone speaks in your catchphrases: "No heroics," "Could've been an email." Like there are five of you.
right: Ask them to use their own words

text: The office manager asks you to pick a color for the new meeting room: "gray," "light gray," or "legendary gray."
The night desk asks you to sign the "after 8 p.m. visitors" log. Your name is on every page this year.
Marketing wants you for the company calendar: 12 months, 12 looks. December: Santa.
Accounting complains everyone now writes in expense reports: "As the legend taught: receipt lost."
Your partner calls at 7:45 p.m.: "Where are you?" At work, though you promised home by 7. Your partner isn't even surprised, and that's worse.
HR proposes a "legend-free hour": nobody may come to you, so staff learn to decide on their own.
Misha wants to photograph your desk for his blog "Desks of the Greats." It's covered in crumbs.
You notice you've switched off the office lights eight evenings in a row. Appoint a "lights person" and go?
Everyone goes quiet when you step into the elevator. You tell the cooler joke. Two laugh, the rest aren't sure they're allowed.
In the smoking area staff are saying you've "gotten too soft." You're around the corner with your tea, listening.
Danya texts at 9 p.m.: "I left at 6 today and the world didn't end!" You're still at the office.
The board proposes "half-time" for your last six months. Meaning: the same workload for half the pay.
Staff are fighting over the AC and ask you to settle it. Some want 20°C, others 26°C.
Platon leaves at 6 p.m. and sticks a note on your laptop: "You can too."
The sysadmin calls at 10 p.m.: a server's down. Can it wait till morning, "like you always say"?
right: Ask him to fix it now

text: At the office party the host announces a "dance with the legend" and asks for volunteers. Forty step up.
Masha's sick this morning, no daycare, your daughter's at work. You have a TV interview at 10. Bring Masha along?
The vet calls mid-board meeting: Ponchik needs his shot today or the next slot is in a month. The meeting's in hour three.
The upstairs neighbor flooded your flat at 9 p.m. You were about to write tomorrow's forum speech.
right: Write the speech at a café

text: You've been in traffic 50 minutes; the meeting's in 10. You could walk 2 km in your suit in the rain.
Your son drops by the office with your grandson because "his class got cancelled." The boy wants to sit in your chair during the meeting.
Renovations at home. At 8 p.m. the workers ask what color the bathroom tiles will be. You've been undecided for three days.
Tuchka ate your speaking notes. Only the last page survives: "And most importantly…"
Mom's visiting and turned up at your office "to see where you vanish to." She's handing out pies at reception.
Your partner suggests a weekend in another city, leaving Friday night. Cheap tickets, and the board meets Monday at 9.
You're on a business-trip train and your compartment neighbor recognizes you. He has 6 hours and many questions.
Your dacha neighbor calls: your fence fell on his beds. He wants you to come "talk right now." You're at a conference.
At 9 p.m. Lyova remembers tomorrow's craft project is due: "My family's jobs." You glue an office model out of boxes.
Snowstorm. The city's at a standstill. You could work from home, but the board expects "the legend in person" at the annual meeting.
Your daughter asks you to talk to her boss, who "doesn't get the word 'balance.'" You know him from conferences.
Neighbors invite you to an evening yard cleanup. You were about to answer board emails.
On the plane a child next to you asks questions the whole way. The mom apologizes. You meant to sleep before your talk.
Your partner calls at lunch: "You forgot our anniversary." You didn't, you planned a surprise tonight. Reveal it?
Ponchik's ill and needs a pill at 11 p.m. and 5 a.m. You have a documentary interview at 9.
The train to the dacha is cancelled. You wanted a weekend offline there. The next one's in 3 hours.
Your sister calls: her son needs college advice, "got five minutes right now?" You're between meetings.
Masha asks you to pick her up from school tomorrow at 1 p.m. At 1 you promised the chairman lunch.
On a business trip the hotel breakfast ends at 9; your talk is at 9:30 across town. Skip breakfast?
Photo in the family chat: the cat's asleep on your embroidery and your grandson drew a rocket on it. You're smiling in the meeting.
Your son asks for help with an investor pitch. He's copying your style, bad jokes included.
right: Praise it and go to bed

text: The taxi's late, the next one's in 20 minutes. Your granddaughter offers you a ride on her scooter.
A neighbor asks you to parrot-sit during your "quiet work day." The parrot squawks "Meeting!" every 5 minutes.
Your partner proposes lights out at 10 and telling each other stories. You want to talk about the board; your partner, cucumbers.
You've started commuting on a scooter. At a light the chairman spots you from his car and honks.
At 3 p.m. Mom sends a 7-minute voice note about a neighbor. You're in a meeting. At the end: "Also, I'm outside your office, let me in."
right: Ask her to wait an hour

text: Lyova asks to sleep over "because you have time now." You do, but there's a live broadcast at 7 a.m.
Before a big broadcast you find a coffee stain on your only white shirt. Forty minutes to air.
right: Buy a new one on the way

text: The family's picking where to spend New Year's. You propose "anywhere, but no laptop." Everyone's stunned.
A neighbor knocks at 10 p.m.: his router's broken and "you know tech." You know reports.
At 7:30 your daughter asks you to pick up her car from the shop "since you're retiring anyway." Retirement is six months away.
Your dacha neighbor sends a photo: the tulips you planted in autumn have bloomed. The meeting suddenly feels very long.
Masha video-calls to show she can ride a bike now. You're at dinner with company partners.
Your partner suggests a run together at 7 a.m. You haven't run in 10 years, and the board's at 9.
Ponchik snuck into your bag and rode to the office. He's discovered mid-meeting, climbing onto the table.
Your sister calls at 10:30 p.m. to talk "about life." You're tired, but you haven't really talked in a year.
First time in the subway in 15 years. The turnstile rejects your card; it's from 2009.
Your son asks if he can sell your car now that you scoot. The car was a gift from the board.
Your partner found an old tape of your talk from 25 years ago. You're in a huge jacket and very serious.
Neighbors are partying at 11 p.m.; you fly at 7 a.m. You get invited "for a slice of cake."
right: Ask them to keep it down

text: At 7 p.m. the workers ask to continue tomorrow at 7 a.m. Your only day off this month.
The dry cleaner mixed up your suit. The one you got is two sizes bigger. Your talk's in an hour.
Masha's voice note: "Promise you'll bake cookies with me every day when you retire?" Every day is a lot.
At 9:30 p.m. your daughter asks if she can drop the grandkids off for the weekend. You wanted quiet; grandkids are noisy joy.
The chairman hears you left a meeting to pick your grandson up from daycare and jokes in front of everyone: "The legend's a nanny now?"
The board moves its session to Saturday at 8 a.m. "since the legend has family on weekdays now." It sounds like a dig.
The CFO calls in the evening while you're bathing your grandson: "Two minutes, just confirm the numbers." The boy splashes.
Platon brings the morning to-do list: 3 items instead of the usual 30. "I learned it from you," he says. The emptiness makes you nervous.
Sonya invites you to her first stand-up as a manager. She promises not to look to you for approval. She breaks within two minutes.
The chairman asks you to write a "10-year strategy," though you're leaving in six months. "Your vision matters."
right: Decline, leave it to the successor

text: The new office wants the "historic cooler" from your first office in its lobby. Movers need your sign-off.
In front of the mirror before your last big speech, you realize you're not nervous. At all. Wisdom or fatigue?
Fyodor calls at 7 a.m.: "Seen the sunrise? No? I see it every day now." Envy or inspiration?
Your successor asks how you knew a decision was right. Honestly: you never knew; you just decided and watched.
Lyova recorded you an alarm: "Wake up, legend, the rocket's waiting." Use it on workdays?
HR asks you to record a "welcome for newcomers" that will play for 5 years after you leave.
Your partner suggests that on your last day you breakfast at the very canteen where you had lunch on your first day. It's still open.
The board sends a survey: "Rate your career from 1 to 10." All you can think to write is "it was good."
Lisa asks: "How do I become a legend?" You think long and answer: "Don't aim for it." She's baffled.
The alarm rings, you switch it off and, for once, deliberately stay in bed 20 more minutes. Lateness is inevitable.
The CFO admits he's copied your work style his whole life and never rested either. He asks how to start.
Breakfast with the whole family at one table for the first time in six months. Your phone buzzes: the board.
Platon asks if he can write a book too: "How I Worked with the Legend." You fear the chapter on your handwriting.
right: Ask him to wait a couple of years

text: You try to recall your happiest workday. Not a deal day, but the day the whole team left at 5 and went for ice cream.
Marketing wants a final video, "The Legend Walks into the Sunset." Literally. The shoot is at dawn "for the light."
Your mentees bring a "time capsule": letters to themselves in 10 years. They ask you to write them one.
The chairman confides: "I want to leave too, but I'm scared." You see yourself three years ago.
You count: 11,000 meetings in your career. How many do you remember? Three. All because of pie.
Zinaida shows up with a cake: "I've closed your last expense report. You can leave in peace."
left: Hug her and cut the cake
right: Thank her and get back to work

text: Your successor turned down an extra board meeting for the first time. The board complains to you. You hide a smile.
Misha asks: "If you started over, would you become a legend again?" You think and say: "I'd eat lunch on time more often."
The board wants you as "honorary chair," no duties. But mandatory photos in annual reports.
Timur proposes merging your mentees and his into a "young leaders' club," with you as guest of honor once a year.
Lyova visits the office and asks if it's true everything will break after you leave. Staff behind him wave: "It won't!"
right: Say they'll miss you a bit

text: For the first time you don't know what next year holds. No plans, no KPIs. Scary and exciting.
On your last evening you pour a cup from the lobby cooler. It gurgles back. You raise the cup and say: "Thank you."
That evening the family asks what you'll do first with your freedom. You say: "Sleep." Everyone in unison: "And then?"
Your partner shows your photo from your first workday and one from today. "You look tired, but the eyes are the same."
In your first department's chat: "So, are we all resting together in six months?" Everyone replies "+", and so do you.
You close your laptop at 6 p.m. and feel not guilt but lightness. Maybe that was the main lesson.
Danya writes: "Today I set a rule for my team: Fridays end at 4." You're proud. Danya's board isn't.
right: Advise him to negotiate with his board

text: Your daughter says she likes who you've become: "You listen now instead of checking email." You want to cry.
On your last evening Platon brings tea and sits beside you: "Can I just sit here?" You sit in silence. Best meeting of the year.
Your first boss sends a card: "You walked a road I never did. Rest for both of us."
Lyova falls asleep in your arms, murmuring: "You're not a legend now, you're just our person." The best promotion of your life.
right: Tuck him in and check email

text: The chairman writes in the evening: "The door is always open. If you get bored, come back." Save the email?
Vika writes: "My intern asked today who taught me to leave on time. I said your name."
The last Friday before a long rest. For the first time in years you've truly made it to Friday. What's next?
Staff give you a big card: a drawing of the office, captioned "We survived. Thank you."
Your partner asks if you regret anything. Honestly: "The dinners I missed." Partner: "There'll be plenty more."
Misha sends his notes on "everything the legend said this year." Last line: "Go home." Underlined three times.
For once the guard doesn't just watch you go; he steps outside and simply stands with you while you wait for your taxi.
right: Shake his hand and get in

text: You get home and the cat greets you at the door. He doesn't care if you're a legend. He wants dinner.
left: Feed him and sit with him

text: Sales asks you to visit a key client one last time "so he doesn't leave along with you." It's a 3-hour drive.
The lawyer brings the last paper to sign: transferring your signing authority. The pen you used for 30 years runs dry.
right: Coax the old pen back to life

text: The receptionist asks what to do with your door plaque: museum, take it home, or toss it?
right: Give it to the office museum

text: Galya peeks in: "Twenty-five years I've cleaned your crumbs. Can I do it one last time while you just sit?"
